newsitem.title: USA: The greatest stock market story ever.
newsitem.headline: The greatest stock market story ever.

text.p: Stocks keep on climbing, despite brief panic sell-offs over inflation, interest rates and worries about the economy's growth, in what may be the greatest stock market story ever told.

The Dow Jones industrial average -- the world's most closely-watched stock market barometer -- this week poked through 6,000 points for the first time. It happened just days before the bull market celebrated its sixth birthday Friday.
The rally started on Oct. 11, 1990, when the index of 30-blue-chip was only 2,365 points.
For the last six years, the market has been feasting on a growing economy and low inflation, which is a perfect recipe for corporate earnings.
In late afternoon trading Friday, the Dow was up 44.73 points at 5,966.40. For the week, it was off 26.46 points.
The market turned cautious after the Dow toyed early this week with 6,000 but was unable to close at that milestone high.
Experts say it has become stylish to be bearish after years of bullishness.
Also, the market is getting ready for the parade of third quarter corporate earnings, which will start next week.
Some Wall Streeters are uncomfortable about the prospect that the growth of corporate earnings may slow, and they fear that the market could be headed for a major correction.
In the last six months, earnings have increased 11 percent compared with last year's torid pace of more than 20 percent.
The leap in the Dow to the 6,000 milestone, which has driven many bears into hibernation and boosted the ranks of bullish traders, is giving the Nervous Nellies another reason to fret.
They reason that often in the past, the market has gotten one more powerful move upward before tipping over.
But the stubborn bull market is attracting more believers.

This week, Morgan Stanley's U.S. Equity Strategist, Byron Wien was the latest high profile market chief to change camp. He now sees another 10 percent rise for stocks, abandoning his forecast that the Dow could crumble by 1,000 points.
Analysts say the market still has upside potential and they are advising investors to stay the course. There are no fundamental reasons why stocks should collapse, they say.

"People didn't believe the market when the Dow was at 3,000 and they thought it was over-priced at 4,000 and they thought there would be a great correction at 5,000 and now they are worried at 6,000 and it's deja vu all over again," said Craig Callahan, chief investment officer at Meridian Investment Management in Englewood, Colo.
He said stocks still have room to go on the upside, and the market could be up another 12 percent by next year because of the continued growth in earnings.
Callahan's target: 6,700 points for the Dow by the end of 1997.

"Stocks are just about where they should be and the market is still within 2 percent of fair value, and slightly to the bargain side, despite the talk that stocks are over-priced," he said. "If interest rates drop then our upside target will get even higher."

Despite jitters over interest rates, inflation and economic growth, stocks have risen every month this year, except in July when the market went through a long-awaited correction of more than 10 percent.
The market has since rebounded nearly 800 points from its summer lows.

Bert Berry, publisher of "No Load Funds*X," a firm in San Francisco that tracks mutual funds said the bull market has been propelled in part by the shrinking supply of stocks due to the popularity of stock indexing.
"The growth of 401K retirement pension plans has led to an explosion of indexing in the S&P Composite index," he said.
Stock indexing involves the buying of all 500 stocks in the S&P index to protect against under-performing the market.

Berry estimated that 10 percent of all of the stocks in the S&P are currently indexed or owned by index mutual funds and retirement pension plans, and the shares are essentially taken out of circulation.
"When you take 10 percent of stocks out of circulation, it drives the other 90 percent higher," Berry said.
The list of S&P stocks includes General Electric Co., International Business Machines Corp., Texaco Inc., Exxon Corp., AT&T Corp. and Procter & Gamble.
Indeed, the supply of cash coming into stock mutual funds is holding strong, which should lessen the threat of a market meltdown.
The Investment Company Institute estimates that cash going into stock mutual funds this year is on pace to nearly double the previous record year of $130 billion set in 1993.
So far in 1996, stock funds have taken in an estimated $177.6 billion and at that rate, they could attract nearly $240 billion for the full year.
